thinkingSteps.title: Aha insight
thinkingSteps.body: To merge k sorted linked lists, we can use a min-heap (priority queue) to keep track of the smallest element from each list. We initially add the first element from each list to the heap. Then, in each iteration, we pop the smallest element from the heap and add it to the merged result. If the popped element has a next element in its original list, we add that next element to the heap. We continue this process until the heap is empty.

solutions.python:
# Merge k Sorted Lists
# Idea: To merge k sorted linked lists, we can use a min-heap (priority queue) to keep track of the smallest element from each list. We initially add the first element from each list to the heap. Then, in each iteration, we pop …
# Line comments below keep the same logic as the NeetCode 150 repo solution.

# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

import heapq


class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: List[ListNode]) -> ListNode:
        min_heap = []
        for i, l in enumerate(lists):
            if l:
                # Heap ops keep min/max ready
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (l.val, i))

        dummy = ListNode()
        current = dummy

        while min_heap:
            val, idx = heapq.heappop(min_heap)
            current.next = ListNode(val)
            current = current.next
            if lists[idx].next:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (lists[idx].next.val, idx))
                lists[idx] = lists[idx].next

        return dummy.next
